title: Athletics at the Olympics: Why the Track is Still the Heart of the Games
summary: The Olympic Games began with running. More than a century later, athletics remains the centrepiece of the world's greatest sporting event. We look at why the track and field programme still defines what the Olympics means.
content:
When the modern Olympic Games were revived in Athens in 1896, the centrepiece of the programme was athletics. Running, jumping, throwing — the events that had defined the ancient Games and that spoke most directly to the idea of human physical excellence. Everything else around them was context. The track was the stage on which the Olympics made its most fundamental argument: that human beings, competing fairly against one another, could produce moments of extraordinary beauty and drama.

More than 130 years later, that argument still holds. When the 100 metres final is run, it is the most watched event of any Olympic Games. When a new world record falls in the field events, the entire stadium holds its breath. Athletics remains the Olympics' most essential sport — the one that most directly answers the question the Games exists to ask.

The 100 Metres: The Fastest Human Alive

No sporting title carries the weight of the Olympic 100 metres champion. The fastest human on Earth. It is the most primitive sporting achievement — who can run from here to there quickest — and it still stops the world for less than ten seconds every four years.

The history of the event traces the history of athletic achievement: Jesse Owens in Berlin 1936, winning four gold medals in front of the Nazi regime that had promised to demonstrate Aryan supremacy. Carl Lewis winning in Los Angeles 1984. Ben Johnson's disqualification in Seoul 1988, which cast a shadow over sprint athletics for a generation. Usain Bolt's three consecutive titles, transforming the event into entertainment as well as athletics.

Field Events: The Overlooked Artistry

The field events — high jump, pole vault, long jump, triple jump, shot put, discus, hammer, javelin — receive less television attention than the track events but contain some of athletics' most technically demanding performances. The pole vault, in particular, is a feat of human ingenuity as much as athleticism — a tool used to transcend what an unaided human body could achieve.

Armand Duplantis's successive world records in the pole vault have brought the event a wider audience than it has had in decades. When he attempts a new record — always at a major championship, always with the bar set at a height no one has cleared before — the moment carries a genuine excitement that the novelty of the attempt creates fresh each time.

Athletics is the Olympics stripped to its essence. No equipment, no team tactics, no complex rules. Just people, trying to run faster, jump higher, or throw further than anyone has ever done before. That simplicity is its power.

The Marathon: The Original Story

The marathon — 42.195 kilometres, run through city streets — connects the modern Olympics most directly to antiquity. The story of Pheidippides running from Marathon to Athens to announce a Greek victory before dying of exhaustion may be legend, but it is a legend that has shaped how we understand endurance, sacrifice, and the limits of human capability.

The Olympic marathon is run on the final day of the Games, its finish inside the main stadium. For the runners crossing that line after more than two hours of racing through city streets, it is an arrival that carries the weight of everything the Olympics represents.

Why It Still Matters

In an era of professional leagues, billion-dollar franchises, and year-round televised sport, the Olympics might seem like a relic — a quadrennial event that struggles to compete with the constant stimulation of modern sports media. And yet the athletics programme still draws enormous audiences, still produces moments that stop the world, still makes athletes into legends in the space of a ten-second sprint or a two-hour marathon.

The reason, perhaps, is that athletics speaks to something universal. Everyone has run. Everyone has jumped. The gap between what we can do and what an Olympic champion can do is vast — but the basic activity is the same. That connection makes athletics uniquely accessible as a spectacle, and uniquely powerful as a symbol of human potential.
